opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, replicability is really the foundation of doing science at all. If I publish a result and nobody else can reproduce it, then what we have is closer to an anecdote than to knowledge. Machine learning has grown incredibly fast, and I think in some ways we've skipped steps that other scientific fields learned the hard way.

There are a few reasons it matters so much. The first is trust. When a paper claims a new state-of-the-art result, other researchers build on it. They cite it, compare against it, and design their next experiments around it. If that result depended on a lucky random seed, an undocumented preprocessing step, or a huge hyperparameter sweep nobody mentions, then a whole line of work can end up built on sand. We've seen cases where careful re-evaluations showed that older, simpler baselines, properly tuned, perform about as well as the shiny new method.

The second reason is understanding. Replicating something forces you to work out which ingredients actually matter. Is the gain coming from the architecture, or from more data, more compute, or a particular evaluation setup? Without that, we're just chasing leaderboard numbers without knowing why things work.

The third is equity and access, which I care a lot about. As models get bigger, fewer and fewer labs can afford to train them, never mind retrain them to check a claim. If replication is only possible for a handful of well-resourced companies, the rest of the community has to take results on faith. That concentrates power and narrows the range of people who can meaningfully take part in the science.

That connects to my work on the environmental side as well. Reporting things like compute used, training time, hardware, and energy consumption is part of making research replicable. It's also part of being honest about the costs. If we don't document those things, we can't reproduce the work, and we can't weigh whether a two-point gain on a benchmark was worth what it took to get there.

So for me, it's not a box-ticking exercise. Sharing code, data, and model details, and being transparent about the experimental process, is how we turn individual results into collective progress. It's how the field corrects itself and stays grounded in evidence rather than hype.

r001.rationale: The response says that if a published result cannot be reproduced by others, it is closer to an anecdote than knowledge, and calls for replication.

r002.rationale: It explains that researchers build on, cite, and design experiments around results, and that an irreproducible result can leave an entire line of work “built on sand.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me it really comes down to what science is supposed to be. If I publish a result and nobody else can reproduce it, then it's not really a scientific finding, it's more like an anecdote. And in machine learning we've gotten into this habit where a paper comes out, it reports a number on a benchmark, and then everyone kind of takes that number at face value and builds on top of it. But very often, when people actually try to rerun those experiments, they get something different. Sometimes the gap is small, sometimes it completely changes the conclusion.

Part of the problem is that there are so many moving pieces. You've got the code, which may or may not be released. You've got the data, which might be proprietary or might have been filtered in ways that aren't documented. You've got random seeds, hyperparameters, hardware differences, library versions. I've seen cases where just changing the random seed gives you a swing bigger than the improvement the paper is claiming. So if we're not reporting variance, if we're not releasing the details, we genuinely don't know whether we're making progress or just getting lucky.

And then there's the environmental and resource angle, which is something I care about a lot. If a result isn't replicable, people spend enormous amounts of compute trying to reproduce it, or worse, building on a foundation that turns out to be shaky. That's wasted energy, wasted carbon, wasted time for grad students who have way fewer GPUs than the labs publishing these results. Replicability is also an equity issue in that sense. If only three organizations in the world can verify a claim, then the field is basically running on trust rather than on evidence.

So when I say replicability is essential, I mean it's the thing that lets us actually accumulate knowledge instead of just accumulating papers. It's about documentation, it's about sharing artifacts, it's about being honest about what you did and what didn't work. That's slower and less glamorous than announcing a new state-of-the-art, but I think it's the only way the field gets to be a real science rather than a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says that if nobody else can reproduce a published result, it is not really a scientific finding.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers building on reported results that may not survive reruns, and warns that this can leave later work built on a shaky foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think replicability is essential because research is cumulative. When you publish a result, other researchers need to be able to understand how you got there, reproduce it, and then build on it. Otherwise, it’s hard to tell whether an improvement comes from the method itself or from something like the data preparation, the computational budget, or even a particular random seed.

In machine learning, the paper alone often doesn’t give you everything you need. The code, the data, the hyperparameters, and the evaluation setup all matter. Making those available lets people test your conclusions in other settings and figure out where they hold and where they don’t. That’s how an individual result becomes something the whole field can learn from.

r001.rationale: It says other researchers need to reproduce a published result independently.

r002.rationale: It describes research as cumulative and says researchers need to reproduce results before building on them; without reproducibility, it is hard to assess the result and the field cannot reliably learn from it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, replicability is what allows research to build on itself. If you publish a result but nobody else can reproduce it, it’s hard to know what actually led to that result. Was it the method, the data, or some detail of the training setup?

In machine learning, there are so many choices that can affect performance. Sharing code, documenting the data, and explaining how you trained and evaluated a model lets other researchers examine those choices and make meaningful comparisons. It also means they don’t have to start from scratch. They can build on what you’ve done, identify limitations, and move the research forward.

r001.rationale: The response says others should be able to reproduce a published result, which communicates independent replicability.

r002.rationale: It says research builds on itself and that results nobody else can reproduce are hard to assess, making them difficult to build on.
